title: Bramble and Saffron's Backward Berry Mystery
markdown:
Morning burst in. Sunlight, golden and gigantic, punched through the stable doors. Bramble the pony’s dappled coat gleamed. His ears, always twitching for adventure, pricked up even higher. But something was wrong. Terribly, utterly wrong. No bird song. No cheerful cheeps or happy chirps. Just silence. A big, gulping silence. Bramble’s hooves, usually tapping a perky rhythm on the dewy grass, felt strangely still.

So he bounded out, a surge of curiosity pushing him. And there, by the mossy fence, was Saffron. Her bright eyes were glued to a dusty forgotten notebook. Not nibbling clover. She was positively, utterly, totally stuck on it. The notebook’s leather cover looked as if it had slept through a thousand badgers’ naps. Saffron blinked, her little goat horns pointing like tiny questioning antennae.

“What’s got your whiskers in a twist, Saffron?” Bramble asked, voice brimming with morning zest.

Just then — plink. A single fat raindrop, plump as a berry, splatted right onto the notebook’s crackling page. And then the ink seemed to sprout. It twisted and twirled, like tiny inky snakes dancing backwards. Utterly bizarre. Completely topsy-turvy.

Bramble blinked his big brown pony eyes. “What in the whirligig is that?”

“It’s writing backward, Bramble,” she bleated, a delighted squeak. “A secret message. A code. Like from a spy.”

But the words swam the wrong way, like trying to catch a greased piglet. Bramble’s mind whirred. He remembered tales whispered by the wise old owl in the library. Brilliant people, like wizards and inventors, sometimes wrote things backward. Mirror writing. “Leonardo da Vinci,” Bramble declared, a spark of brilliance igniting his thoughts. “He wrote in mirror script. We have to read this backward. Like a proper puzzle.”

They huddled together, Bramble’s warm comforting pony breath mingling with Saffron’s sweet minty goat scent. Saffron, with her incredibly sharp eyes, spotted something glinting nearby: a tiny dewdrop-covered leaf, still clinging to a spider’s silk thread. “Hold it up, Bramble. Let’s use the sunlight. Reflect it.”

With utmost care Bramble positioned the notebook close to the leaf. The pale morning sunlight, catching the tiny dewdrop, bounced the strange backward writing back at them. Slowly, gloriously, as the light danced and played, the words began to untangle themselves.

The twelve Sparkleberries are gone. Find them before the sun sets.

Bramble gasped, a puff of astonished air escaping his nostrils. The Sparkleberries. Those were the tiny, almost invisible, shimmering fruits that grew on the highest branches of the Whispering Willow. They were the secret ingredient that made the birds sing their most beautiful morning songs. Without them, the whole world was left with that dreadful gulping silence.

But the willow was tall, and the sun was already climbing. Saffron nudged him, bright eyes dancing. “We have to find them, Bramble. Right now. This is important.”

Bramble felt a thrilling jolt shoot through his sturdy pony body. He tossed his head, dappled coat shimmering like a thousand tiny mirrors. “You’re right, Saffron. This is our mission.”

They set off at a brisk trot, hooves thumping a determined beat. First they checked the orchard, where the apples hung like little lanterns. No sparkle. Then the ditch where the blackberries grew fat and ordinary. Still no shimmer. A cheeky magpie eyed them from a fence post, looking far too pleased with himself.

“You wouldn’t happen to have borrowed twelve very shiny berries, would you?” Saffron asked.

The magpie only clicked his beak and flew off toward the willow, a suspicious glitter in his tail.

So they followed. At the Whispering Willow the highest branches were empty, leaves trembling as if they had just been robbed. But the grass below was dotted with tiny pale lights — Sparkleberries, rolled and scattered, some already half-hidden under moss. Bramble lowered his head so Saffron could scramble up his mane like a very determined mountain goat. She plucked them one by one from the crooks of the branches the magpie had missed, and Bramble nosed the fallen ones into a careful pile.

Twelve. The last one winked like a dewdrop that had decided to stay.

They tucked the berries back among the willow’s highest leaves, where the birds could find them. For a moment nothing happened. Then a single robin tried a note, thin as a thread. Another joined. Then the whole dawn chorus arrived late, loud, and gloriously out of order, as if the morning had been holding its breath and had finally remembered how to sing.

Bramble and Saffron stood in the returning music, notebook closed, dewdrop leaf discarded, the backward mystery now facing the right way. The magpie, looking slightly less pleased, practised an innocent whistle from a safer tree. Today, it turned out, was going to be amazing.
